opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, Ravid, it's great to be here.

I think the breakthrough is less about transformers being dramatically better at vision tasks in isolation and more about what their adoption did to the field. For most of the 2010s, vision and language ran on separate architectural tracks. Vision had convolutional networks with strong inductive biases like locality and translation equivariance, and language moved from RNNs and LSTMs to transformers. When the Vision Transformer showed that you could cut an image into patches, treat them like tokens, and get very competitive results with essentially the same architecture used for text, it unified the two communities.

That unification matters for a few reasons. First, it made it much easier to share ideas, training recipes, and scaling insights across modalities. A lot of what we learned about scaling language models transferred more or less directly. Second, it opened the door to multimodal models. If images and text are both sequences of tokens going through the same kind of network, combining them becomes much more natural, and that's the foundation for many of the vision-language systems we see today.

Third, and this is something I've thought about a lot, it challenged our assumptions about what inductive biases we actually need. The conventional wisdom was that convolution's built-in priors were essential for vision. ViT showed that with enough data and compute, a more generic architecture can learn those regularities on its own.

That said, I'd add a caveat, and it's partly what motivated our ConvNeXt work. When we went back and modernized a standard ResNet, borrowing design choices and training techniques from transformers, we found convolutional networks could match or beat them on many benchmarks. So part of the transformers' apparent advantage came from better training recipes and design decisions rather than from attention itself. The real breakthrough, in my view, is the shift in mindset toward general, scalable architectures and shared practices across domains, more than the triumph of one specific operation over another.

r001.rationale: The response says ViT treated image patches as tokens using the architecture used for text, unifying the two communities, and notes that images and text can share token-based networks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I think the reason I regard it as such an important moment is not really about the architecture itself. It's about what it did to the field's assumptions.

For almost a decade, computer vision had this very strong inductive-bias story. We believed that locality, translation equivariance, hierarchical feature maps, all these things baked into convolutional networks, were essential to learning from images. They were treated as almost principled, like you needed them because images have this spatial structure. And then ViT came along and basically said, take an image, chop it into sixteen-by-sixteen patches, flatten them, and feed them into a model that was designed for language, with essentially no image-specific priors. And it worked. Not immediately on ImageNet from scratch, but with enough data and enough scale, it matched and then surpassed what we had.

That was humbling, and I think productively so. It forced us to ask which parts of our architectures were actually doing the work and which were just historical accident. That question is actually what motivated ConvNeXt for me. We wanted to know, is the transformer really winning because of attention, or is it winning because of a whole bundle of design decisions that came along for the ride, the training recipe, the patchify stem, the larger kernels, fewer activations, layer norm instead of batch norm? And when we modernized a ResNet step by step with those ideas, it caught up. So the honest answer is that the breakthrough wasn't that attention is magic. It was that it exposed how much we had been leaving on the table.

The second thing, and I think this is ultimately bigger, is unification. Once vision uses the same building block as language, you suddenly get this shared infrastructure. The same scaling laws start to apply, the same optimization tricks transfer, and more importantly you can put images and text in the same sequence and train one model on both. CLIP, the multimodal large language models we have now, none of that is easy if vision and language live in architecturally separate worlds. The transformer became a kind of common currency.

And the third thing is scaling behavior. Convolutional networks, at least the way we trained them, tended to saturate. Transformers kept improving with more data in a way that was very clean and predictable, and that matters enormously if you believe, as I increasingly do, that a lot of progress is going to come from scale and from data rather than from clever architectural tweaks.

So if I summarize it, the importance is really threefold. It challenged a set of beliefs we held a little too confidently, it unified vision with the rest of machine learning, and it gave us a path that scales. Whether attention specifically survives in the long run, I'm honestly not sure. But that shift in mindset I think is permanent.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers let vision and language share a building block and enable images and text to be placed in the same sequence, identifying their representational unification as a benefit.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest breakthrough is that transformers gave us a much more unified way to approach different modalities. For a long time, computer vision was built around convolutional networks, while language processing used different architectures. With vision transformers, we saw that an architecture that worked well for language could also work extremely well for images.

That matters beyond performance on an image classification benchmark. When images and text can be processed with similar building blocks, it becomes much easier to bring them together in one model. Ideas and improvements can also transfer more directly between the two fields.

It also challenged our assumptions about what a vision model needs. Convolutions encode useful structure about images, especially locality and translation equivariance. Transformers showed that, with enough data and the right training, we can learn much of that structure instead of explicitly building it into the architecture. That doesn’t mean those inductive biases are no longer useful. But it opens up a much broader design space, and I think that shift is very important.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers let images and text use similar building blocks, making it easier to bring them together in one model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important breakthrough is that transformers gave computer vision a much more general architecture. For a long time, we relied on convolutional networks, which build in strong assumptions about images, especially locality and translation equivariance. Those assumptions are useful, but vision transformers showed that, with enough data and the right training, we could learn much of that structure instead.

That also brought vision and language closer together. You can represent an image as a sequence of patches and process it with an architecture similar to one used for text. That makes it easier to share ideas across fields and to build models that work with both images and language.

But I wouldn’t interpret this as saying that attention is always better than convolution. For me, the exciting part is that it pushed us to revisit which architectural choices actually matter, which advantages come from training and scale, and how much prior structure we really need.

r001.rationale: The response says images can be represented as patch sequences processed with an architecture similar to text, bringing vision and language closer together.
